Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 1–3:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾. We have discussed the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijāʾ, the letters of the alphabet that open some surahs) in al-Baqarah. ﴿A constriction from it﴾, meaning a tightness of breast about conveying it, along with the denial of your people. It has also been said that ḥaraj here means doubt, so its interpretation is like His saying: ﴿So do not be among those who doubt﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 60]. ﴿That you may warn﴾ is connected to anzala (was sent down). ﴿And a reminder﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with a hidden verb whose implied sense is "that you may warn and remind, a reminder," because dhikr here means tadhkīr (reminding). It may also be in the nominative as the predicate of a hidden subject (khabar mubtada'), or in the genitive by coordination with the position of li-tundhira, meaning "for warning and for reminding." ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾: qalīlan is in the accusative governed by tadhakkarūn, meaning "you remember with little remembrance." Mā is extra, for emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 4–6:

﴿We destroyed it, and Our punishment came upon it﴾. It has been said that this is an inversion (al-maqlūb), and its meaning is: Our punishment came upon it, so We destroyed it. It has also been said that the meaning is: We intended to destroy it, and Our punishment came upon it, because the arrival of punishment comes before the destruction, so it is not correct to join it to the destruction with the particle fa (then). It is possible that ﴿fa-jāʾahā baʾsunā﴾ is a resumed clause (istiʾnāf) given as an explanation (tafsīr) of the destruction, in which case no strained interpretation is needed. The intended meaning is: We destroyed its people, and Our punishment came upon them, and the noun that was omitted (al-muḍāf) is understood from the evidence in the words ﴿or while they were resting at noon﴾. [The verse's words] ﴿bayatan aw hum qāʾilūn﴾: bayatan is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning "passing the night" (bāʾitīn), that is, at night. Qāʾilūn is from al-qāʾilah (midday rest), that is, during the day. Punishment struck some of the earlier disbelievers at night and some during the day, and the particle aw here indicates variety.

﴿Their claim﴾ (daʿwāhum), meaning: their calling out and their pleas for help were only an acknowledgment that they had been wrongdoers (ẓālimūn). It has also been said that the meaning here is the claim they used to make concerning their religion, and when the punishment came to them they confessed that they had been wrongdoers in that.

﴿They were sent to﴾ (ursila ilayhim): the verb has been attributed to the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-l-majrūr). The meaning of the verse is that God questions the nations about how they responded to their messengers, and questions the messengers about how they were answered.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 11–18:

﴿We created you, then We fashioned you﴾. It is said: the meaning is that We intended your creation and your fashioning. ﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. It is also said: We created your father Adam, then We fashioned him. The interpretation (ta'wil) was needed so that the conjunction (al-'atf) would be sound. ﴿"What prevented you from prostrating"﴾: the particle "lā" is extra (za'idah), for emphasis (li-l-tawkid). ﴿When I commanded you﴾: some of the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence, usul al-fiqh) cited this as evidence that a command (amr) entails obligation (wujub) and immediacy (al-fawr), and that is why punishment was incurred for not hastening to prostrate. ﴿He said, "I am better than him"﴾: this is a reason (ta'lil) by which Iblis justified his refusal to prostrate. It implies an objection to God, may He be exalted, in commanding the superior to prostrate to the inferior, in his own view. Through this objection Iblis disbelieved, since his disbelief was a disbelief of denial (kufr juhud). ﴿"Then go down from it"﴾: that is, from heaven. ﴿He said, "Because You have led me astray"﴾: the "fa'" is for causation (lil-ta'lil), and it relates to a suppressed oath (fi'l qasam mahdhuf), its estimated sense being: "I swear by God, because of Your leading me astray, I will surely lead the children of Adam astray." The "mā" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah). It is also said to be interrogative (istifhamiyyah), but the presence of the alif in "mā" with the preposition refutes this. ﴿Your path﴾: he means the path of guidance and good, and it is in the accusative of place (zarf). ﴿Then I will certainly come to them from before them﴾: that is, from the four directions. This is an expression for his being empowered over the children of Adam in whatever way he is able. Ibn 'Abbas said: "From before them" is the world, "from behind them" is the Hereafter, "from their right" are the good deeds, and "from their left" are the sins. ﴿Reproached﴾: from dha'amahu, with hamza, when he blamed him. ﴿Expelled﴾: that is, driven away wherever it occurs.

It is also said to be interrogative (istifhamiyyah), but the presence of the alif in "mā" with the preposition refutes this. ﴿Your path﴾: he means the path of guidance and good, and it is in the accusative of place (zarf). ﴿Then I will certainly come to them from before them﴾: that is, from the four directions. This is an expression for his being empowered over the children of Adam in whatever way he is able. Ibn 'Abbas said: "From before them" is the world, "from behind them" is the Hereafter, "from their right" are the good deeds, and "from their left" are the sins. ﴿Reproached﴾: from dha'amahu, with hamza, when he blamed him. ﴿Expelled﴾: that is, driven away wherever it occurs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 20:

﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾. When one speaks a hidden speech and repeats it, that is waswasa (whispering). The meaning of "waswasa lahuma" (whispered to them) is that he cast this speech to them. ﴿That he might reveal to them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾, i.e., that he might make apparent what was hidden of their nakedness. The lam in his saying "liyubdiya" (that he might reveal) is for causation (ta'lil) if the uncovering of them was a purpose for Iblis, or for consequence (sayrura) if that occurred without his intending it. ﴿The tree﴾: it was mentioned in al-Baqara [2:35]. ﴿Except that you become angels﴾, i.e., lest you become angels. From this, whoever said that the angels are superior to the prophets derived evidence. The reading "malakayn" with a kasra on the lam has also been transmitted, and this reading is strengthened by his saying: "wa malikin la yubla" (and a king who does not decay).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 21–27:

﴿And he swore to them both﴾: that is, he swore to them: "Indeed, I am among the sincere advisers to you." The oath of Iblis is expressed with the form *mufa'ala* (the verbal pattern denoting reciprocity, usually between two parties), either because he strove hard in it, or because he swore to them and they swore to him that they would accept his advice. ﴿So he led them both on﴾: that is, he brought them down to eating from the tree. ﴿With deception﴾: that is, he deceived them by his oath to them, because they thought he would not swear falsely. ﴿Then their private parts became apparent to them both﴾: that is, their clothing was removed and their nakedness appeared. They had not seen it in themselves, nor one of them in the other. It was said that their clothing had been a light that prevented them from looking at each other. ﴿They began to join together over themselves leaves from the Garden﴾: that is, they attached some of it to another so that they might cover themselves with it. ﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾: this call may have been through an angel, or without an intermediary. ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾: an acknowledgment and a request for forgiveness and mercy, and these are the words by which Allah accepted their repentance. ﴿Go down﴾: what follows it is mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿Therein you will live﴾: that is, on the earth. ﴿Garments﴾: that is, the clothing that covers. The meaning of "We sent down" is "We created." It was also said that what is meant is that We sent down that from which clothing comes, namely rain. Some jurists used this verse as evidence for the obligation to cover the private parts. ﴿And as adornment (rish)﴾: that is, clothing of beauty, and it is a metaphor taken from the feathers (*rish*) of a bird. ﴿And the garment of righteousness﴾: a garment, like the saying of people: "May Allah clothe you in the shirt of His piety." It was also said that the garment of righteousness is what one protects oneself with in war, such as coats of mail and the like. It was also read in the nominative (*raf'*), as an inchoative (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being the clause "that is better." ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾: the reference is to the clothing that was sent down. This verse comes as a digression following the mention of the exposure of the private parts and the joining of leaves over them, in order to show His favor in creating clothing. ﴿He strips off from them both their clothing﴾: that is, he was the cause of stripping their clothing from them. ﴿From where you do not see them﴾: meaning in most cases. Whoever said that jinn are not seen has used this verse as evidence, and sound hadiths have come about seeing them, so the verse is understood as referring to the majority, in order to reconcile it with the hadiths.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 28–30:

﴿وَإِذَا فَعَلُواْ فَٰحِشَةً﴾ It was said: it refers to what the Arabs used to do, circumambulating the House (the Ka'bah) naked, men and women alike. It may also be understood in general terms, covering all indecencies. ﴿They said: "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah commanded us to do it."﴾ They offered two false excuses: first, the imitation of their forefathers; second, their fabrication against Allah.

﴿وَأَقِيمُواْ وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ It was said: the intended meaning is bringing forth the intention and sincerity to Allah; and it was said: it means performing the prayer and turning toward the qiblah in it. ﴿at every place of prostration (masjid)﴾ That is, in every place of prostration, or at the time of every prostration; the first is more apparent. The meaning is the permissibility of prayer in every place, like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The earth has been made a mosque (masjid) for me."

﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ An argument for the resurrection of the Hereafter from the first origination.

﴿A party He has guided﴾: the first (party) is in the accusative governed by "guided" (hada), and the second is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, which is explained by what follows it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 31:

﴿Take your adornment﴾. It is said: what is meant is the clothing that covers, and those who hold that covering the private parts in prayer is obligatory have taken this as evidence. It is also said: what is meant is adornment beyond mere covering, such as beautifying oneself for the Friday prayer with the best clothes, using the siwak (tooth-stick), and wearing perfume. ﴿And eat and drink﴾. The command in both is for permissibility (ibahah), because some of the Arabs used to forbid themselves certain foods. ﴿And do not be excessive﴾, that is, do not eat in excess of what is needed. The physicians said: all of medicine is gathered in this verse. It is also said: do not be excessive by eating what is forbidden.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 32:

﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾ is a denial of its prohibition. What Allah has prescribed for His servants is clothing and food. Some of the Arabs, when they performed the pilgrimage, would strip off their garments and circumambulate the Ka'bah naked, and they would forbid fat and milk. So this was revealed in refutation of them. ﴿Purely for those who believe in the life of this world, and exclusively for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ means: the adornment and the good things in this world are for those who believe and for others besides them, while in the Hereafter they are exclusively for them, to the exclusion of others. It has been read as khāliṣatan (خالصةً) in the accusative, as a state (ḥāl), and in the nominative, as a predicate following a predicate, or as the predicate of an implied subject (mubtada').

﴿And sin﴾ is general, covering every sin. ﴿And that you say about Allah﴾ means that you invent lies against Him concerning prohibition and other matters. ﴿Should there come to you﴾: the word إِمَّا (*immā*) is the conditional إن (*in*, the conditional particle) with the superfluous (*al-zāʾida*) ما (*mā*) joined to it for emphasis. It takes the emphatic heavy nūn (*al-nūn al-shadīda al-muʾakkida*). The response to the condition (*jawāb al-sharṭ*) is ﴿whoever is mindful﴾, the verse.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 37–39:

﴿So who is more unjust﴾ (mentioned in al-An'am) ﴿than those who will receive their share of what was decreed for them in the Book﴾, i.e., what was written for them of provision and other things will reach them. ﴿They have strayed from us﴾, i.e., they have disappeared. ﴿Enter among nations﴾, i.e., enter the Fire in the company of nations, or along with nations. ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another﴾ (tala-hiqu, i.e., they caught up with one another and gathered together). ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾. What is meant by "the first of them" are the leaders and chiefs, and "the last of them" are the followers and the lowly. The meaning is that the last of them asked Allah to double the punishment for the first of them, because they misled them. It does not mean that they said this to them directly; rather, it is like your saying, "So-and-so said to so-and-so such-and-such," meaning he said it about him, even if he did not address him with it. ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you earned."﴾ i.e., you had no superiority over us in faith and piety that would require our punishment to be more severe than yours; rather, we and you are equal. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾ is either from the words of the first to the last, or from the words of Allah Most High to all of them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 40–41:

﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: their deeds will not ascend to heaven. The second: they will not enter Paradise, since Paradise is in heaven. The third: the gates of heaven will not be opened for their souls when they die, as they are opened for the souls of the believers. ﴿Until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾, that is, until the camel enters the hole of the needle. The meaning is: they will not enter Paradise until what cannot happen happens, so they will never enter it. ﴿A bed (mihad)﴾: a bedding (firash). ﴿Coverings (ghawash)﴾: coverings (aghita).

﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiraḍiyya) placed between the subject and predicate, to show that what is required of good deeds is within a person's capacity and ability. ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾: that is, whoever had resentment toward his brother in this world, We will remove it from him in Paradise, and they will become brothers and companions. He said "nazaʿnā" (We removed) in the past tense, although the action is future, to affirm that it will certainly occur, so that it is expressed in the form used for what has already happened. The same applies to everything that follows in this passage in the past tense, which will take place in the Hereafter, such as ﴿The companions of Paradise will call out﴾, ﴿The companions of the Heights will call out﴾, ﴿The companions of the Fire will call out﴾, and other examples. ﴿Who guided us to this﴾: a reference to Paradise, or to what required faith and piety. ﴿That this is Paradise﴾, ﴿That we have found﴾, ﴿That the curse of God﴾, and ﴿That peace﴾: each of the "an" (that) in these may be the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna" (muthaqqala), in which case there is an implied pronoun, or it is a particle introducing an explanation of the meaning of the speech. ﴿What our Lord promised us is true﴾: the object of "waʿada" (promised) is omitted, either because it is understood from the object of "waʿadanā" (promised us), or because the promise is left unrestricted so that it includes both reward and punishment. ﴿Then a caller called out﴾: that is, a announcer made it known, and he is an angel. ﴿And between them is a barrier﴾: that is, between Paradise and the Fire, or between their people; the latter is preferable, based on His saying: ﴿So a wall with a gate was set up between them﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 13]. ﴿The Heights (al-A'rāf)﴾.

Ibn 'Abbās said: it is a hill between Paradise and the Fire. It was also said: it is the wall of Paradise. ﴿Men﴾: they are the people of the Heights. It is reported in a hadith that they are a people from the children of Adam whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so they did not enter Paradise nor the Fire. It was also said: they are people who went out to jihad without the permission of their parents, were martyred, and were thus prevented from entering Paradise because of their disobedience to their parents, yet were saved from the Fire due to their martyrdom. ﴿They will recognize each by their marks﴾: that is, they will recognize the people of Paradise by their sign of brightness of faces, and the people of the Fire by their sign of blackness of faces, or by other signs. ﴿And they will call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you"﴾: that is, the greeting of peace from the people of the Heights to the people of Paradise. ﴿They have not entered it, though they aspire﴾: that is, the people of the Heights have not entered Paradise, while they still hope to enter it later. ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the Heights, meaning when they see the companions of the Fire, they supplicate God not to place them with them. ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men﴾: meaning among the disbelievers who are in the Fire, and they say this to them in rebuke. ﴿Your gathering﴾: it may mean their gathering of wealth, or their large number. ﴿And what you used to be arrogant about﴾: that is, your arrogance toward the Fire, or your arrogance toward returning to the truth. Here "mā" is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya), and the "mā" in His saying ﴿what good it was﴾ is interrogative or negative.

This is because the disbelievers used to swear in this world that God would not show mercy to the believers and would not care for them; then what they had said was shown to be false. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 54–55:

﴿The Most Merciful settled upon the Throne﴾. Some people took it according to its apparent meaning, among them Ibn Abi Zayd and others. Others interpreted it to mean "intended," as in His saying: ﴿Then He turned toward the heaven﴾. Had that been the meaning, it would have said "then He turned toward the Throne." The Ash'aris interpreted it to mean that istawa means istawla (took dominion) through sovereignty and power. The truth is: belief in it without modality (takyif), for safety lies in submission. How excellent is the statement of Malik ibn Anas in answer to the one who asked him about this: "The istiwa' is known, the modality (kayfiyyah) is unknown, and asking about this is an innovation (bid'ah)." Something like the statement of Malik has been narrated from Abu Hanifa, Ja'far al-Sadiq, and al-Hasan al-Basri. The Companions and the Successors did not speak about the meaning of istiwa'; rather, they refrained from it, and for this reason Malik said, "Asking about this is an innovation."

﴿He causes the night to cover the day﴾, that is, He makes the night follow the day. It may bear both meanings; so said al-Zamakhshari. The root of the word is from ghisha' (covering), meaning one of them becomes a covering for the other, veiling it, so the darkness of the night covers the light of the day.

﴿Seeking it swiftly﴾, that is, quickly. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) relative to the night, meaning the night seeks the day and overtakes it.

﴿Surely, to Him belong the creation and the command﴾. It has been said: "the creation" means the created things, and "the command" is the verbal noun of amara, yamuru. It has also been said: "the creation" is the verbal noun of khalaqa, and "the command" is the singular of "affairs" (umur), as in His saying: ﴿To Allah all affairs are returned﴾. Both are correct.

﴿Blessed be﴾ comes from barakah (blessing). It is an indeclinable verb, for the Arabs never used a present-tense form for it.

﴿Humbly and secretly﴾ is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), and likewise khawfan wa tam'an (fearfully and hopefully). Khafyah comes from ikhfa' (concealment), and it has been read as khiyfah, from khawf (fear).

﴿The transgressors﴾ are those who exceed the limit. It has been said that here it refers to raising the voice in supplication and going to excess in it.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 56:

﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope.﴾ Allah combined fear and hope so that the servant may be both fearful and hopeful, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾ [al-Isra: 57]. The cause of fear is knowing Allah's might and the severity of His punishment, and the cause of hope is knowing Allah's mercy and the greatness of His reward. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Inform My servants﴾ [al-Hijr: 49]. Whoever knows Allah's bounty hopes in Him, and whoever knows His punishment fears Him. For this reason a hadith says: "If the fear and hope of the believer were weighed, they would balance." However, it is recommended that the servant, throughout his life, let fear predominate in order to lead him to performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, and that hope predominate at the approach of death, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you should die except while he has good expectation of Allah the Exalted."

Know that fear has three degrees. The first: that it be weak, passing through the heart without affecting the inner or outer self; the existence of this is like its non-existence. The second: that it be strong, so that it awakens the servant from heedlessness and carries him to uprightness. The third: that it intensify until it reaches despair and hopelessness, and this is impermissible. The best of matters is their middle. People in fear have three stations: the fear of the common people is of sins; the fear of the elite is of the final outcome; and the fear of the elite of the elite is of the preordained past, for the final outcome is built upon it. Hope has three degrees. The first: hope in Allah's mercy together with taking the means to it by performing obedience and abandoning disobedience; this is the praiseworthy hope. The second: hope accompanied by negligence and disobedience; this is delusion. The third: that hope grow until it reaches a sense of security; this is forbidden. People in hope have three stations: the station of the common people is hope for Allah's reward; the station of the elite is hope for Allah's good pleasure; and the station of the elite of the elite is hope for meeting Allah, out of love for Him and longing for Him. ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. The feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith) was dropped from "qarib" (near). It is a predicate about "mercy" under the interpretation of mercy as "compassion," "showing mercy," or "pardon"; or because the feminine of "mercy" is not real (metaphorical); or because it is the attribute of an omitted noun, its estimate being "a thing that is near"; or by the reckoning of relation, meaning "possessing nearness." It is also said that "qarib" here is not a predicate about "mercy," but rather an adverb of place/time for it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 57–58:

﴿The winds as glad tidings﴾. It is recited as "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, because these are the winds that bring rain. The plural is consistently used in the Qur'an when the winds bring mercy, and the singular when they bring punishment. From this comes the hadith (a report of the Prophet's sayings): "O Allah, make them winds (riyahan) and do not make them a single wind (rihan)." It is also recited in the singular, and the intended sense is the genus. It is recited as "nashran" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the shin. On this reading it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). It is also recited with a damma on the nun, as the plural of "nushur." It was said to be the plural of "manshur." It is also recited with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the shin, as "nushr," which is a lightened form of the damma, like "rusul" and "rusul." It is recited with a ba' in place of the nun, and then it derives from "bushra" (good news).

﴿Before His mercy﴾, that is, before the rain. ﴿They carry﴾, that is, they bear, ﴿heavy clouds﴾, because they carry water and become heavy with it. ﴿We drive it﴾: the pronoun refers to the clouds. ﴿To a dead land﴾, meaning one with no vegetation because of severe drought. Its meaning is the same wherever it occurs. ﴿Then We send down water by it﴾: the pronoun refers to the clouds or to the land, with the ba' being used as a particle of place. ﴿Thus We bring forth the dead﴾: this is an image for bringing the dead out of their graves, and for bringing crops out of the earth. This comparison occurs in the Qur'an in several places, such as "Thus is the resurrection" and "Thus is the coming forth."

﴿And the good land﴾ is the noble land of good soil. ﴿And that which is wicked﴾ is the opposite, such as salt flats and the like. ﴿Comes forth only by the permission of its Lord﴾ is an expression for ease and goodness, while barrenness is the opposite. It may be that the intended meaning is what the apparent wording requires, so that it completes the meaning before it concerning rain. Or it may be an image for hearts. It was said that on this reading, "the good" is the heart of the believer and "the wicked" is the heart of the disbeliever. It was also said that they refer to the intelligent person and the dull person.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 59–62:

﴿مِّنْ إِلَـٰهٍ غَيْرُهُ﴾ Al-Kisa'i read ghayrihi with a kasra wherever it occurs, following the wording (lafz). Others read it with a damma, following the position (mawdi'). ﴿عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, or the day of their destruction. ﴿ٱلْمَلأُ﴾ means the nobles of the people (ashraf al-nas). ﴿لَيْسَ بِي ضَلٰلَةٌ﴾ He said ḍalala and did not say ḍalal, because ḍalala is more specific than ḍalal, just as when someone is told "You have dates (tamr)," and replies "I have not a single date (tamra)," thereby generalizing the negation. ﴿أُبَلِّغُكُمْ﴾ It is recited with tashdid and with takhfif, and the meaning is one. In terms of i'rab it is either a description (sifa) of a messenger, in the nominative position, or a new independent clause (isti'naf). ﴿وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مَا لاَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ That is, from His attributes, His mercy, and His punishment.

Others read it with a damma, following the position (mawdi'). ﴿عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, or the day of their destruction. ﴿ٱلْمَلأُ﴾ means the nobles of the people (ashraf al-nas). ﴿لَيْسَ بِي ضَلٰلَةٌ﴾ He said ḍalala and did not say ḍalal, because ḍalala is more specific than ḍalal, just as when someone is told "You have dates (tamr)," and replies "I have not a single date (tamra)," thereby generalizing the negation. ﴿أُبَلِّغُكُمْ﴾ It is recited with tashdid and with takhfif, and the meaning is one. In terms of i'rab it is either a description (sifa) of a messenger, in the nominative position, or a new independent clause (isti'naf). ﴿وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مَا لاَ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ That is, from His attributes, His mercy, and His punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 63–72:

﴿Do you wonder﴾ The hamza (alif of interrogation, a particle of denial/rebuke) is for censure, and the waw is for conjunction, and the element conjoined to is omitted; as if he said: "Do you deny and wonder that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord through a man among you?", i.e., through the tongue of a man among you. ﴿in the ship﴾ is connected to "with him," and the sense is: "settle with him in the ship." It is also possible that it is connected to "We saved him." ﴿blind﴾ is the plural of "blind," and it refers to blindness of the heart. ﴿their brother﴾ means one of their tribe. It is in apposition to Nuh, and Hud is a substitute for it or an explanatory apposition; likewise "their brother Salih" and what follows, and whatever is like it wherever it occurs. ﴿the chiefs of those who disbelieved﴾ It is restricted here to disbelief because among the chiefs of the people of Hud there was one who believed, namely Murthid ibn Sa'd, unlike the people of Nuh, among whom there was no believer, so the word "chiefs" was used without restriction. ﴿trustworthy﴾ may mean that he is trustworthy in conveying revelation, or that they had known him for trustworthiness and truthfulness. ﴿successors after the people of Nuh﴾ i.e., you were made to succeed them in the land, or He made you rulers. ﴿and increased you in stature within creation﴾ They were huge of body; the shortest of them was sixty cubits and the tallest was a hundred cubits. ﴿the bounties of God﴾ means blessings wherever it occurs. ﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we may worship God alone?"﴾ They found it strange that God be made one, while acknowledging His lordship; therefore Hud said to them: ﴿There has already fallen upon you﴾ i.e., there has become due and been decreed upon you ﴿a punishment and wrath from your Lord﴾. ﴿Do you dispute with me about names that you have named﴾ referring to the idols: i.e., you dispute with me about worshipping things that are merely names. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and by his saying "you have named them" he means that you and your fathers gave them names, which indicates they are created, so they cannot be gods; or "you named them gods" without any proof that they are gods, so your claim is false. Thus the dispute, on the first interpretation, concerns worshipping them, and on the second concerns calling them gods. The word "names" on the first interpretation means the named things, and on the second means the act of naming. ﴿cut off (dabir)﴾ has been mentioned in al-An'am [6:45].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 73:

﴿A clear proof from your Lord.﴾ That is, a manifest sign, and it is the she-camel. It was attributed to God as an honour to her, or because He created her without a male. They had asked Salih (peace be upon him) to bring it forth for them from a rock, and they pledged to him that they would believe in him if he did so. The rock split open and the she-camel came out of it while they watched. Then she gave birth to a young one, and some of them believed in him while others disbelieved. ﴿This is a sign for you﴾ That is, a miracle indicating the truth of Salih's prophethood. The prepositional phrase (al-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "ayah," because if it were placed after it, it would be a descriptive qualifier (sifah). ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾ That is, do not strike her and do not drive her away.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 74:

﴿And He settled you in the land﴾. Their land lay between al-Sham (Syria) and al-Hijaz, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions entered it. He (ﷺ) said to them, peace be upon him: "Do not enter upon these punished people except while you are weeping," lest there befall you the like of what befell them. ﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾, meaning you build palaces on the flat land. ﴿And you hew out the mountains as houses﴾, meaning you take houses in the mountains. They used to dwell in the palaces in summer and in the mountains in winter. And "buyutan" (houses) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), like your saying: "I sewed this garment as a shirt" (khattu hadha al-thawb qamisan).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 75–79:

﴿Those among them who believed﴾: a substitute (badal) for "those who were deemed weak." ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that in which you believed.﴾ The reason they did not say "we disbelieve in what he was sent with," as the others said, is so that it would not amount to an acknowledgment of his prophethood. ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾: the hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were pleased with it, even though only one of them did it, namely al-Ahmar (al-Ahmar). ﴿The quake﴾: the cry (al-sayha) wherever it occurs. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 80–84:

﴿When he said to his people⟩ The governing element of "idh" (when) is the implied "We sent" (arsalna), or it is a substitute (badal) for Lut. ﴿No one in the worlds has preceded you in it⟩, that is, no one among the worlds has done it before you. The first "min" (from) is extra (za'ida), and the second is either partitive (lil-tab'id) or generic (lil-jins). ﴿So the answer of his people was not⟩ [al-Naml: 56] and so on: that is, they turned away from answering his words and moved to ordering his expulsion and the expulsion of his family. ﴿People who keep themselves pure⟩, that is, who keep themselves far from indecency. ﴿Among those who remain behind⟩, that is, among those who perish. It has been said: among those who stayed behind in their dwellings and so were destroyed, or among the survivors of their kin. It is said "ghabara" meaning he perished, and it is also said meaning he remained. He said "al-ghabirin" (those who remain behind) in the masculine plural, giving precedence to the men who remained behind. ﴿And We rained upon them a rain⟩, meaning stones. Those of them who were outside their lands were struck by them, and the lands were overturned along with those who were in them.

Clear Evidence from your Lord: that is, a manifest sign. The Qur'an does not specify which sign it was (the sign of Shu'ayb).

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: They used to cheat in measure and weight, so Shu'ayb was sent to forbid them from this. Here "al-kayl" (measure) means the vessel by which one measures, to match the scale (al-mizan), as in Hud, "the measure and the scale." It is also permissible that both "al-kayl" and "al-mizan" are verbal nouns (infinitives).

﴿And do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾: It is said that this is a prohibition against robbery and highway banditry. This was among their practices: they would sit on the roads, turning people away from following Shu'ayb and threatening them if they followed him.

﴿and barring [people]﴾: That is, you prevent people from the way of Allah, which is faith. The pronoun in "bihi" refers either to the path or to Allah.

﴿and seeking to make it crooked﴾: This is mentioned in Al 'Imran [99].

﴿Or you will return to our religion﴾: That is, one of two things will certainly happen: either their expulsion [of you], or your return to the religion of disbelief. If it is asked: the word "return" (ʿawd) to something implies that one had done it before, so their saying "you will return to our religion" implies that Shu'ayb and those with him were initially on the religion of their people, then left it, and their people then demanded that they return to it, which is impossible, for prophets are protected from disbelief both before and after prophethood. The answer to this is given in two ways. First: stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah, that "ʿāda" may mean "ṣāra" (became), so it does not require that the earlier state existed before the state they became. Second: stated by al-Zamakhshari, that what is meant is those who believed with Shu'ayb, not Shu'ayb alone; they included him in the address with them, just as they included him in the address in their saying, "We will surely drive you out, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you." Thus the plural was used for the singular in the address with "return." The same answer applies to the statement: ﴿We would be returning to your religion after Allah has rescued us from it. It would not be for us to return to it﴾.

﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾: The hamza is interrogative and expresses denial, and the waw is for the circumstantial state. Its sense: "Would we return to your religion while it would be for us to return to it while we are unwilling?"

﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion﴾: That is, if we returned to it, we would have fallen into a great matter of fabricating against Allah. This is a disavowal of returning to it.

﴿And it would not be for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills﴾: This is submission to the decree of Allah, in a manner of good manners toward Allah and attributing matters to Him. When he disavowed their religion, he informed them that Allah judges over them by what He wills, of return or abandonment, for hearts are in His hand; He turns them however He wills. If it is said: this holds regarding his people, but as for himself, it does not, for he is protected from disbelief? The answer: he said that out of humility and good manners toward Allah, the Exalted, and submission to His command, like the saying of our Prophet (ﷺ): "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion," although he knew that He would make it firm.

﴿Our Lord, decide between us﴾: That is, judge.

﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾: That is, as if they had never dwelt in their homes.

﴿So how could I grieve over a disbelieving people﴾: That is, how could I grieve over them when they deserved what befell them of punishment because of their disbelief.

﴿with adversity and hardship﴾: This has been mentioned before.

﴿We replaced the evil with good﴾: That is, We replaced adversity and hardship with bounty, testing them in both states.

﴿until they increased﴾: That is, they multiplied and grew in their persons and wealth.

﴿and said: "Adversity and ease have touched our fathers"﴾: That is, such things happened to our fathers, and it did them no harm; so it is by coincidence, not by intent of testing.

﴿And it would not be for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills﴾: This is submission to the decree of Allah, in a manner of good manners toward Allah and attributing matters to Him. When he disavowed their religion, he informed them that Allah judges over them by what He wills, of return or abandonment, for hearts are in His hand; He turns them however He wills. If it is said: this holds regarding his people, but as for himself, it does not, for he is protected from disbelief? The answer: he said that out of humility and good manners toward Allah, the Exalted, and submission to His command, like the saying of our Prophet (ﷺ): "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion," although he knew that He would make it firm.

﴿Our Lord, decide between us﴾: That is, judge.

﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾: That is, as if they had never dwelt in their homes.

﴿So how could I grieve over a disbelieving people﴾: That is, how could I grieve over them when they deserved what befell them of punishment because of their disbelief.

﴿with adversity and hardship﴾: This has been mentioned before.

﴿We replaced the evil with good﴾: That is, We replaced adversity and hardship with bounty, testing them in both states.

﴿until they increased﴾: That is, they multiplied and grew in their persons and wealth.

﴿and said: "Adversity and ease have touched our fathers"﴾: That is, such things happened to our fathers, and it did them no harm; so it is by coincidence, not by intent of testing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 96–100:

﴿Blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾: that is, through rain and crops. ﴿Or do they feel secure﴾: as for the one who reads the waw with sukun, then it is "aw" (or), the conjunctive particle; and as for the one who reads it with a fatha, then it is the waw of conjunction, into which the interrogative hamza of reproach (hamzat al-tawbikh) has entered, just as it entered upon the fa' in His saying ﴿Do they then feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾: that is, His gradual seizing (istidraj) and His taking of the servant from where he does not perceive. ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land﴾: that is, those who dwell in it. ﴿That if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins﴾: this is the subject (fa'il) of "has it not become clear," and the purpose of the verse is a warning (wa'id). ﴿And We seal over their hearts﴾: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "afflicted them," because it carries the meaning of the future tense; or it is a resumption (munqati') on the sense of a warning. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be coordinated upon "those who inherit the land," or upon what the meaning of "or has it not become clear" indicates, as if he said: they are heedless of guidance, and We seal over their hearts.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil (commentary on Surah 7, verses 102–105):

﴿And We found not in most of them any covenant﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of the towns, and the meaning is: We found them breaking covenants.

﴿It is right for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth﴾. As for whoever reads ʿalayya with the shadda (intensive doubling), where it is the first person pronoun (yāʾ of the speaker), the meaning is clear: Moses said, "It is incumbent upon me that I should not say about Allah except the truth." The position of "an lā aqūla ʿalā" here is in the nominative case, as the predicate of ḥaqīq, or ḥaqīq is the predicate and it is the subject; the reverse is also possible.

As for whoever reads ʿalā with the lightened pronunciation (takhfīf), the position of "an lā aqūla" is in the genitive case, governed by the preposition, and ḥaqīq is an attribute of rasūl (messenger). Regarding the meaning in this case there are two views. The first: ʿalā here carries the sense of bāʾ (bi), so the sense of the statement is: "A messenger who is fit to not say about Allah except the truth." The second: the meaning of ḥaqīq is "eager" (ḥarīṣ), and for this reason it is followed by ʿalā.

﴿Indeed I have come to you with a clear sign from your Lord﴾, that is, with a miracle that testifies to my truthfulness, namely the staff, or the category of miracles in general.

﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾, that is, let them go with me to the Holy Land, the homeland of their forefathers. This is because, when Joseph (ʿalayhi al-salām) died, Pharaoh overpowered the Children of Israel, enslaved them, until Allah rescued them through the hand of Moses. The interval between the day Joseph entered Egypt and the day Moses entered it was four hundred years.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 108–110:

﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white﴾. Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) was very dark-complexioned. He showed his hand to Pharaoh, then put it back into his garment (jayb), and then drew it out, and it was white, exceedingly white, like milk or even whiter. It was also said that it was luminous and radiant like the sun, and that after that it would return to the color of his body. ﴿To the onlookers﴾: an intensifier in describing the whiteness of his hand. The people used to gather to look at it and to marvel at it. ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer."﴾ This statement is related here as coming from the chiefs (al-Mala), and in al-Shuʿara' it is related as coming from Pharaoh. It is as if he said it and they said it with him, or he said it and they agreed with him, as is the custom of the companions of kings in following what the king says. ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾: that is, to expel you from it by fighting or by stratagems. It was also said that the intended meaning is the expulsion of the Children of Israel, who were their servants, so the land would be ruined by the departure of the servants and the cultivators from it. ﴿So what do you advise?﴾: this is from the statement of the chiefs or from the statement of Pharaoh, and it derives from the meaning of mu'amara, that is, consultation, or from al-amr, which is the opposite of al-nahy (prohibition).

﴿أَرْجِهْ﴾ (Put them off). Whoever reads it with a hamzah (the glottal stop), it is from *arja'tu al-rajul* ("I delayed the man") when one delays him. So the meaning is: delay the two of them until we consider their matter. It was also said that *al-irja'* (postponement) here means imprisonment. Whoever reads it without a hamzah, it may be understood as the hamzated form with the hamzah softened, or as from *al-raja'* (hope), meaning "give him hope." As for the vowelling of the *ha'* with a *damma* or a *kasra*, these are two dialectal forms. As for its being read with a sukun, perhaps the reciter applied the *wasl* (connected reading) the way of the *waqf* (pause).

﴿حَاشِرِينَ﴾ (gatherers) means the police (*al-shurtah*), that is, those who gather the sorcerers.

﴿وَجَآءَ ٱلسَّحَرَةُ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ (And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh). It was said that there is an omitted element here, indicated by the context of the speech: that he sent to the sorcerers.

﴿إِنَّ لَنَا لأَجْراً﴾ (Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward). Whoever reads it with two hamzahs, *a-inna*, it is an interrogative. Whoever reads it with one hamzah, it may be a declarative statement, or an interrogative from which the hamzah has been dropped. *Al-ajr* here means *al-ujrah* (wage). They asked Pharaoh for it if they overcame Moses. Pharaoh granted them it, and increased them in nearness to him and in standing with him.

﴿وَإِنَّكُمْ لَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ﴾ (And indeed you will be among those brought near). It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the meaning of *na'am* (yes), as if he said: "We will give you a reward and bring you near."

The number of the sorcerers differed greatly, from seventy men to seventy thousand, and all of this has no basis in sound transmission.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 117:

﴿Throw down your staff﴾ When he threw it, it became a great serpent, of the size of the rope. It was also said that it grew until it surpassed the elephant. ﴿It swallows﴾ i.e., it devours ﴿what they fabricate﴾ i.e., what they had contrived by their falsehood and lying. It is narrated that the serpent devoured all the valley of their ropes and staffs, and Musa extended his hand toward it, and it became a staff as it had been. So the sorcerers knew that this was not from magic, and that it was not within the power of human beings, and they believed in Allah and in Musa, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 124–130:

﴿Surely I will cut off your hands﴾ (the verse): a threat from Pharaoh to the magicians. The Qur'an does not state that he carried it out, but it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others that he did carry it out. The meaning of "crucifixion" (ṣalb) was mentioned in the discussion of differences concerning the verse of al-Maʾida [5:33].

﴿They said: "Indeed, to our Lord we will return."﴾ That is, we do not care about death, since our return is to our Lord.

﴿"And you resent us only because we believed."﴾ That is, you find fault with us only for our faith.

﴿"So that they may cause corruption in the land."﴾ That is, that they may ruin the kingdom of Pharaoh and his people and oppose his religion.

﴿"And that they may leave you"﴾ is coordinated with "so that they may cause corruption," or is in the subjunctive by an implied "an" after the waw. ﴿"And your gods"﴾: it has been said that Pharaoh had set up idols for the people to worship and had made himself the supreme lord, which is why he said: ﴿"I am your most high lord"﴾ [al-Naziʿat 79:24]. On this view, "your gods" are those idols. ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-ālihataka," meaning your worship and your submission to you.

﴿"Indeed, the earth belongs to God."﴾ This is a reason for patience, which is why Moses commanded them to be patient. The earth here means the earth of this world, as in His words: ﴿"and He will make you successors in the land"﴾. It has also been said that it means the land of Pharaoh. So Moses first indicated to them victory in His words: ﴿"He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants"﴾, then stated it explicitly in His words: ﴿"Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act"﴾ (the verse). ﴿"Then He will see how you act"﴾ is an exhortation to steadfastness and obedience.

"With the years" (bil-sinin): that is, drought and famine.

﴿But when good came to them﴾, the verse: when fertility and prosperity came to them, they said, "This is ours by right, and we deserve it." And when drought and hardship came to them, they took omen from Musa (Moses), meaning they said, "This is because of his ill omen." If it is asked: why did He say ﴿when good came to them﴾ with *idhā* (إذا) and the definite *al-ḥasanah* (the good), but ﴿if an evil afflicts them﴾ with *in* (إن) and the indefinite *sayyi'ah* (evil)?

The answer: the occurrence of good is frequent, and the occurrence of evil is rare. So what occurs frequently is made definite with the *lām* of previous reference (al-ʿahd). He used *idhā* because it implies certainty, and he mentioned evil with *in* because it implies doubt, and he made it indefinite to indicate its rarity.

﴿Behold, their omen is only with God﴾, meaning: their portion and share, which was decreed for them of good and evil, is with God. The word is taken from the augury of birds (zajr al-ṭayr), and then it was applied to whatever befalls a person. The purpose of the verse is to refute them regarding what they attributed to Musa of ill omen.

*Mahmā* (مهما) is the conditional *mā* with the additional *mā* joined to it, as in *ayna-mā* (wherever). Then the alif was changed to a *hā'*. It is said that it is a simple, not compound, noun. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 137–140:

﴿The people who were being oppressed﴾ are the Children of Israel. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾ are al-Sham (Greater Syria) and Egypt. ﴿Which We had blessed﴾ means with fertility and abundance of provision. ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾ means it was accomplished for them and became established. The "word" here is what was decreed for them in eternity. It was also said that it is His saying: ﴿And We wished to show favor to those who were oppressed in the land﴾. ﴿And what they had been building﴾ means what they were constructing (ya'rishun, "to build"). It was also said that it refers to vineyards and the like; on the first view the verb is from al-'arsh (structures or thrones), and on the second it is from al-'arish (trellises).

﴿They said, "O Musa, make for us a god"﴾ means: make for us an idol that we may worship, just as these people worship their idols. When the account of Musa with Pharaoh was complete, he began the account of his dealings with the Children of Israel from here until His saying: ﴿And when We lifted the mountain over them﴾ [al-A'raf: 171].

﴿Destroyed﴾ is from al-tabbar, which means ruin. ﴿And that He preferred you over the worlds﴾, and what follows it is mentioned in al-Baqarah [47].

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 7, verses 142–145**

﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights﴾. It is narrated that the thirty were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da, and the ten after them were the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. This is the detail of the forty mentioned in al-Baqara. ﴿The appointed time of his Lord﴾, meaning the time set for him to converse with Him at Mount Tur. ﴿Be my successor﴾, meaning: be my deputy over the Children of Israel during my absence. ﴿He said: My Lord, show me Yourself﴾. When Musa heard the speech of Allah, he longed to see Him, so he asked for that, as the poet said:

"The longing is at its most joyful one day, when the abodes draw near to the abodes."

The Ash'arites used this to argue that seeing Allah is rationally possible, and that if it were impossible, Musa would not have asked for it, since the prophets, peace be upon them, know what is permissible for Allah and what is impossible. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted Musa's request to see Allah in two ways. The first is that he asked only to rebuke those who went out with him from the Children of Israel and who demanded to see Allah, ﴿So they said: Show us Allah plainly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153]. Musa said this so that they would hear the answer forbidding it and would then be silent. The second is that the meaning of "show me" is "let me look at You", i.e., "make Yourself known to me in a clear and manifest way." Both interpretations are far-fetched, and the second is even further and weaker, for if seeing were not the intended meaning, He would not have said to him, "Look at the mountain," and so on.

﴿He said: You will not see Me﴾. Mujahid and others said: Allah said to Musa, "You will not see Me, because you cannot bear it. But I will manifest Myself to the mountain, which is stronger and firmer than you. If it remains steady and can endure the awe of Me, then it is possible that you may see Me; and if the mountain cannot endure it, then you are even less able to." According to this view, Allah made the mountain an example for Musa. Some said: the meaning is "I will manifest Myself to you upon the mountain." This is weak, since His words refute it: ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾.

Having established this, the words of the Most High, "You will not see Me," are a negation of seeing, but they contain no evidence that seeing is impossible. He only made the reason for the negation the inability of Musa to bear seeing, not its impossibility. Had seeing been impossible, the answer would have been a stern rebuke and reproof, as Allah said to Nuh: ﴿So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46]. The prohibition of seeing Allah applies only in this world, owing to the weakness of the human constitution for that. As for the Hereafter, the Book of Allah and the Sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ) have explicitly affirmed that it will occur, and none denies it except an innovator (mubtadi', one who introduces a belief not grounded in the Sunna). Between the People of the Sunna and the Mu'tazila there is a long dispute over the question of seeing Allah. Many narratives are related about this story, which I have omitted because they are unsound and because they contain corrupt statements.

﴿When His Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾. The word dakk means "crushed," so it is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, like your saying "I struck the amir." Dakk and daqq are close relatives, both meaning "to be broken into pieces." It was also read as dakā' with a long vowel and a hamza, meaning "a flat, levelled ground." It is also said that the top of the mountain went away and most of it remained. It is said that it was pulverized until it became dust. It is said that it sank into the earth and reached the sea.

﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾, meaning he fainted.

﴿I repent to You﴾, meaning: I repent of asking to see You in this world, for I cannot bear it. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾, meaning: the first of his people or of the people of his time, or it is an expression of exaggeration in being the earliest to faith.

﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾. This is a general expression intended to be particular, for all the messengers shared with him in prophethood. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 146:

﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth﴾ The signs: here it may be intended that they refer to the Qur'an and other scriptures, or to the signs and proofs. The "turning away" (al-sarf) is meant as restraining them from understanding them and from believing in them, as a punishment for their arrogance. It has also been said: the "turning away" means preventing them from nullifying them.

﴿And the meeting of the Hereafter﴾. It is permissible that this is the construction of a verbal noun (maṣdar) with its direct object (maf'ūl bih), meaning "their meeting the Hereafter," or the construction of the verbal noun with an adverbial noun of time or place (ẓarf). ﴿And the people of Moses took﴾: they are the Children of Israel. ﴿after him﴾: that is, after his absence at Mount Sinai (al-Ṭūr). ﴿from their ornaments﴾: with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a shadda on the lām, it is the plural of ḥilī, like thady and thidy. It is also read with a kasra on the ḥā' for ittibā' (vowel harmonization, assimilating the vowel to the following one), and read with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and sukūn on the lām. Ḥilī is the name for what is adorned with gold and silver. ﴿a calf (jasad)﴾: that is, a body without a soul. Its case is in apposition (badal). ﴿It had a lowing (khuwār)﴾: khuwār is the sound of cattle. Al-Sāmirī had taken a handful of dust from the hoofprint of Gabriel's horse on the day the sea was crossed, and threw it into the calf, so it had a lowing. It is also said that Iblīs would enter the belly of the calf and cry out within it, so a lowing was heard from it. ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾: this is a refutation of them and a nullification of their corrupt belief in worshipping it. ﴿They took it﴾: that is, they took it as a god, and the second object is omitted because it is known. Likewise it is omitted in His saying: "and the people of Moses took." ﴿And when they regretted (suqita fī aydīhim)﴾: that is, they repented. It is said: "suqita fī yad fulān" when a person is unable to achieve what he wants, or falls into what he dislikes. ﴿in anger (asafan)﴾: deeply grieved over what they had done. It is also said: greatly angry, as in His saying: ﴿when they angered Us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55]. ﴿Evil is what you have done in my place (bi'sa mā khalaftumūnī)﴾: that is, you took my place. The agent of bi'sa is an implied pronoun explained by mā, and the name of what is condemned is omitted. The one addressed is either the people who worshipped the calf along with al-Sāmirī, since they worshipped other than God during Moses' absence from them, or the leaders of the Children of Israel, such as Hārūn, peace be upon him, since they did not restrain those who worshipped the calf. ﴿Have you hurried ahead of your Lord's command?﴾: its meaning is: have you hastened past the command of your Lord, which was to wait for Moses until he returned from Mount Sinai. When they saw that the matter had been completed, they thought Moses, peace be upon him, had died, so they worshipped the calf. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾: he cast them down, due to the bewilderment and distress that overcame him, out of anger for God over the worship of the calf. ﴿And seized his brother by the head﴾: that is, by the hair of his head. ﴿dragging him toward himself﴾: because he thought Hārūn had been negligent in restraining those who worshipped the calf. ﴿son of my mother (ibna umm)﴾: Hārūn was the full brother of Moses. He addressed him by their mother because that calls forth more tenderness and compassion. It is also read "ibni umm" with a kasra, as an idāfa to the first person pronoun ya', and the ya' is dropped; with a fatḥa, the ya' is dropped by analogy to khamsata 'ashara (fifteen), where the two words are made into one word and become indeclinable. ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, do not think that I am one of them, or do not hold against me in your heart what you hold against them, meaning the companions of the calf. ﴿Anger from their Lord and humiliation﴾: that is, anger in the Hereafter and humiliation in this world. ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses (sakata 'an Mūsā al-ghaḍab)﴾: that is, it became calm. Nuskha has the pattern fu'la in the sense of maf'ūl (what is copied). ﴿for their Lord they are fearful (yarhabūn)﴾: that is, they fear. The lām is introduced because the object has been placed first, as in His saying: ﴿you interpret dreams (lil-ru'yā ta'burūn)﴾ [Yūsuf: 43]. It is said: "suqita fī yad fulān" when a person is unable to achieve what he wants, or falls into what he dislikes. ﴿in anger (asafan)﴾: deeply grieved over what they had done. It is also said: greatly angry, as in His saying: ﴿when they angered Us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55]. ﴿Evil is what you have done in my place (bi'sa mā khalaftumūnī)﴾: that is, you took my place. The agent of bi'sa is an implied pronoun explained by mā, and the name of what is condemned is omitted. The one addressed is either the people who worshipped the calf along with al-Sāmirī, since they worshipped other than God during Moses' absence from them, or the leaders of the Children of Israel, such as Hārūn, peace be upon him, since they did not restrain those who worshipped the calf. ﴿Have you hurried ahead of your Lord's command?﴾: its meaning is: have you hastened past the command of your Lord, which was to wait for Moses until he returned from Mount Sinai. When they saw that the matter had been completed, they thought Moses, peace be upon him, had died, so they worshipped the calf. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾: he cast them down, due to the bewilderment and distress that overcame him, out of anger for God over the worship of the calf. ﴿And seized his brother by the head﴾: that is, by the hair of his head. ﴿dragging him toward himself﴾: because he thought Hārūn had been negligent in restraining those who worshipped the calf. ﴿son of my mother (ibna umm)﴾: Hārūn was the full brother of Moses. He addressed him by their mother because that calls forth more tenderness and compassion. It is also read "ibni umm" with a kasra, as an idāfa to the first person pronoun ya', and the ya' is dropped; with a fatḥa, the ya' is dropped by analogy to khamsata 'ashara (fifteen), where the two words are made into one word and become indeclinable. ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, do not think that I am one of them, or do not hold against me in your heart what you hold against them, meaning the companions of the calf. ﴿Anger from their Lord and humiliation﴾: that is, anger in the Hereafter and humiliation in this world. ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses (sakata 'an Mūsā al-ghaḍab)﴾: that is, it became calm. Some readers recited it this way too. Al-Zamakhsharī said: His saying "sakata" is like "as if the anger had been saying to him: throw down the tablets and drag your brother by the head," and then it became silent about that. ﴿And in their copy (nuskhatihā)﴾: that is, in what was copied from them. Nuskha has the pattern fu'la in the sense of maf'ūl (what is copied). ﴿for their Lord they are fearful (yarhabūn)﴾: that is, they fear. The lām is introduced because the object has been placed first, as in His saying: ﴿you interpret dreams (lil-ru'yā ta'burūn)﴾ [Yūsuf: 43]. Al-Mubarrad said: it is connected to a verbal noun whose implied sense is "their fear of their Lord."

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 7, verses 155–156:

﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men﴾ — i.e., from among his people — ﴿seventy men﴾. He brought them with him to Mount Tur to hear God's speech to Musa. They said: "Show us God openly," so the quake (al-rajfah) seized them as a punishment for their saying. It is also said that the quake seized them because of their worship of the calf, or because of their silence about its worship. The first view is more preferred, based on His saying: ﴿So they said, "Show us God openly," and the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) seized them for their wrongdoing.﴾ It is possible that it was a quake of death or of fainting, and the first (view) is more evident, based on His saying: ﴿Then We revived you after your death.﴾

﴿"If You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me as well"﴾ — it is possible that "law" (if) here is for wishing, meaning: they wished that he and they had died before that, because he feared the agitation of the Children of Israel against him if he returned to them without these seventy. It is also possible that he said this in a manner of humble supplication and submission to God's command, as if he said: "If You had willed to destroy us before that, You would have done so, for we are Your servants and under Your domination, and You do what You will." And it is possible that he said it in a manner of humble supplication and longing, as if he said: "If You had willed to destroy us before today, You would have done so, but You have granted us well-being and preserved us, so do for us now what You promised us, and revive these people whom the quake seized."

﴿"Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"﴾ — i.e., will You destroy us and all the rest of the Children of Israel for what the foolish ones did, those who asked to see (God) and those who worshipped the calf? The meaning of this is a presentation of his argument and a disavowal of the foolish ones' act, and a longing toward God that He not punish everyone collectively.

﴿"It is none but Your trial; You send astray thereby whom You will"﴾ — i.e., all matters are in Your hand. The meaning of this is an excuse for the act of the foolish ones, for it occurred by God's decree and will.

﴿"We have turned back to You"﴾ — i.e., we have repented. These words that Musa, peace be upon him, spoke are only an appeal for compassion, a longing toward God, and a humble supplication to Him. They do not imply anything of what the ignorant have imagined of harshness in his saying: "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?", because we have already explained that he said that only as an appeal for God's compassion and as a disavowal of the act of the foolish ones.

﴿He said: "My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will"﴾ — it was said: the reference by "that" is to those whom the quake seized, but the correct view is that it is a general statement, in which they are included along with others. It was read as "man asa'" (with sin and an open hamza, from " isa'ah", wrongdoing), but some reciters rejected this and said it is a scribal distortion (tashif).

﴿"And My mercy encompasses all things"﴾ — it is possible that he means His mercy in this world, in which case it is specific in being mercy and general in "all things," because the believer and the disbeliever, the obedient and the disobedient, all receive God's mercy and bounty in this world. It is also possible that he means the mercy of the Hereafter, in which case it is specific in "all things," because mercy in the Hereafter is restricted to the believers. It is also possible that he means the kind of mercy in an absolute sense, in which case it is general in mercy and in "all things."

﴿"So I will write it for those who fear (God)"﴾ — if the mercy mentioned is the mercy of the Hereafter, then it is without doubt specific to those for whom God has written it, namely the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). If it is the mercy of this world, it is also specific to them, because God gave them victory over all nations, raised their religion above all religions, and established them in the land in a way not granted to others. If it is in the absolute sense, then His saying "I will write it" is a specification of the absolute.

﴿"And those who believe in Our signs"﴾ — i.e., who believe in all the books and the prophets, and this belongs to none but this community.
