Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 157:

﴿Those who follow the Messenger﴾. This description specifies the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Some of them said: When God said, "My mercy encompasses all things," everyone hoped for it, even Iblis. But when He said, "I will decree it for those who fear Me," Iblis despaired, may Allah curse him, and only the Jews and Christians remained. ﴿The Prophet, the unlettered﴾, meaning the one who neither reads nor writes. That is among the greatest proofs of his prophethood (ﷺ), for he brought abundant knowledge without reading or writing. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write one with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. Some of them said: the word ummi (unlettered) is derived from umm (mother), and it was also said: from ummah (community). ﴿Whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. The subject of the verb in "they find him" refers to the Children of Israel, and likewise the pronoun in "with them." The meaning of "they find him" is that they find his description and attributes written. Here we shall mention what is found in the Torah and the Gospel and the reports of earlier generations concerning our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Among these is what is recorded in al-Bukhari and others, that in the Torah there is a description of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger; I have named you the one who relies (al-Mutawakkil). You are not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets. You do not repay evil with evil, but you pardon and overlook. I will not take him until he establishes the crooked religion by their saying, 'There is no god but Allah,' so that by him blind eyes, deaf ears, and veiled hearts are opened."

Among what is in the Torah, and what the People of the Book agree upon and which remains in their hands to this day: the angel descended to Abraham and said to him, "In this year a boy will be born to you named Isaac." Abraham said, "O Lord, would that Ishmael might live to serve You." God said to Abraham, "That is for you; your request concerning Ishmael has been granted. I will bless him, make him fruitful, increase him and magnify him greatly, with ... (bmadh madh)." The interpretation of these letters is Muhammad. (Sefer Genesis [17].)

Among what is in the Torah: the Lord, exalted is He, came from Mount Sinai, rose up from Sa'ir, and appeared from the mountains of Paran. By Mount Sinai is meant the place where Moses (peace be upon him) conversed with God; Sa'ir is the place of 'Isa (Jesus), and Paran is Makkah, the place of birth and mission of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning of what is mentioned about God's coming, rising and appearing is the manifestation of His religion through the hands of the three prophets connected with those places. Its explanation is in the Book of Isaiah, addressed to Makkah: "Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of God has risen upon you. Darkness covers the earth, and gloom the nations, but the Lord will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you. Nations will walk toward your light and kings toward the brightness of your rising. Lift up your eyes around you and see: they are gathered to you, and the armies of the nations come to you." And in some of their books: "The heavens have been split by the splendour of the praised Muhammad, and the earth is filled with his praise, for he appeared with the deliverance of his community."

Among what is in the Torah, Sefer Genesis [16]: when Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, was angered by Sarah, an angel appeared to her and said, "O Hagar, where do you wish to go, and from where have you come?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarah." He said to her, "Return to Sarah, and you will conceive and bear a son named Ishmael; he will be the eye of the people, his hand will be above all, and the hands of all will be stretched out to him in submission." The point of this statement as evidence for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is that what the angel promised her, that her son's hand would be above all and all hands stretched to him in submission, appeared only with the mission of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the manifestation of his religion and the elevation of his word; this was not the case for Ishmael or anyone else before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Also in the Torah: the Lord will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, and whoever does not hear that prophet's words that he conveys from God, God will take vengeance upon him. The indication of this statement is clear: the sons of Ishmael are brothers of the sons of Isaac, and God has taken vengeance upon the Jews who did not hear the words of Muhammad (ﷺ), such as the Banu Qurayzah, the Banu Qaynuqa' and others.

Also in the Torah: God revealed to Abraham (peace be upon him): "I have answered your prayer concerning Ishmael, I have blessed him, and he will beget twelve great ones, and I will make him a great nation."

Also in the Gospel: Christ said to the disciples, "I am going away from you, and the Paraclete will come to you, who does not speak of his own accord; he says only what is said to him." By this God, glorified is He, described our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 3-4]. The interpretation of Paraclete is that it is derived from praise (hamd), and the name of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) is Muhammad and Ahmad. It was also said that the meaning of Paraclete is "the intercessor whose intercession is accepted."

Also in the Torah: his birth in Makkah, his dwelling in Taybah, and his community are "the praisers" (al-hammadun). The proof of this is that his community recites "Al-hamdu lillah" in their prayers many times each day and night. And from Shahr ibn Hawshab, a similar account concerning the Islam of Ka'b al-Ahbar, who was from Yemen, from Himyar: Ka'b informed him of his affair and how it came about. It was said that his father was among the believing People of the Torah in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and was among their great and best men. Ka'b said: He was among the most knowledgeable people about what Allah revealed to Moses in the Torah and in the books of the prophets, and he kept nothing from me of what he knew. When his death approached, he called me and said: "My son, you know that I have kept nothing from you of what I knew, except that I withheld from you two pages in which there is mention of a prophet who is to be sent, and his time has drawn near. I disliked telling you of this, for I do not feel safe for you after my death that some of these liars may come out and you follow him. I have cut them from your book and placed them in this niche you see, and sealed them with clay. Do not touch them or look at them in your lifetime, and leave them in their place until that prophet comes out. When he comes out, follow him and look into them, for God will increase you in goodness by this."

When my father died, nothing was more beloved to me than that the period of mourning should end, so that I could look at what was in the two pages. When the mourning ended, I opened the niche, took out the two pages, and in them was: Muhammad, Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Seal of the Prophets, there is no prophet after him; his birth is in Makkah and his emigration to Taybah; he is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets; he does not repay evil with evil but repays with good, and he pardons, forgives and overlooks. His community are the praisers, who praise God over every height and in every state, whose tongues are made humble by takbir, and God will give victory to their prophet against all who oppose him. They wash their private parts with water, gird their waists, carry their Gospels in their chests, eat their offerings in their bellies, are rewarded for them, and their mercy among themselves is the mercy of children of one mother and father. They are the first of the nations to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection; they are the foremost, the brought near, and the intercessors whose intercession is accepted. When I read this, I said to myself: By God, nothing has taught me anything better for me than this. I remained as long as God willed, until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, but between me and him were distant lands, cut off, and I could not reach him. It reached me that he had appeared in Makkah, showing himself at times and hiding at others. I said: This is he. But I feared what my father had warned me of and what he had cautioned me about regarding the liars, and I longed to clarify and verify. I continued in this until it reached me that he had come to Madinah. I said to myself: I truly hope it is he, and I began seeking a way to him, but it was not granted to me until it reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had died. I said to myself: Perhaps he was not the one I was thinking of.

Then it reached me that a caliph had taken his place, and I did not wait long before his armies came to us. I said to myself: I will not enter this religion until I know whether they are the ones I was hoping for and awaiting, and I will observe their conduct and deeds and where their end will lead. I kept postponing and delaying this to clarify and verify, until 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came to us. When I saw the prayer and fasting of the Muslims, their righteousness and fulfillment of covenants, and what God did for them against their enemies, I knew they were the ones I had been waiting for, and I resolved within myself to enter the religion of Islam.

By God, one night I was on a roof when a man of the Muslims was reciting the Book of God until he reached this verse: ﴿O you who have been given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down, confirming what is with you, before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their heels, or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath; and the command of God is ever executed﴾ [al-Nisa': 47]. When I heard this verse, I feared God that I would not reach the morning before my face was turned around on my back, and nothing was more beloved to me than morning. So I went to 'Umar at dawn and embraced Islam.

When they were returning to Syria, Ka'b said to 'Umar: "O Commander of the Faithful, it is written in the Book of God that this land in which the Children of Israel lived and whose people they were will be conquered by the hand of a righteous man, merciful to the believers and firm against the disbelievers, whose secret is like his public, whose public is like his secret, whose word does not contradict his deed, and to whom the near and the far are equal in truth; his followers are monks by night and lions by day, merciful, connected, and generous to one another." 'Umar said to him: "May your mother be bereaved! Is what you say true?" He said: "Yes, by Him who sent down the Torah to Moses, and whoever hears what you say knows that it is true." 'Umar said: "Praise be to God, who has honored us, raised us, ennobled us, and shown us mercy through Muhammad (ﷺ), by His mercy which encompasses all things."

Among these is the letter of Farwah ibn 'Amr al-Judhami to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He was one of the kings of the Arabs in Syria, and he wrote to him: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. To Muhammad, Messenger of Allah, from Farwah ibn 'Amr. I affirm Islam and believe it. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the servant of Allah and His messenger, and that he is the one whom 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) gave good news of." Heraclius seized him when news of his Islam reached him and imprisoned him, and he said: "By God, I will never leave the religion of Muhammad." For you know that he is the Prophet whom 'Isa ibn Maryam foretold, but you were eager for your kingdom and loved its survival. Caesar said: "He has spoken the truth, and by the Gospel."

This is supported by what al-Bukhari and Muslim transmitted of the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Heraclius and Heraclius's question about his circumstances and character (ﷺ). When he was informed of them, he knew that he was the Messenger of Allah, and said: "He will rule the place of my feet, and if I could reach him, I would wash his feet." (al-Bukhari, Kitab Bad' al-Wahy.)

From the report of Zayd ibn Aslam from his father, which is with us by chain, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) went out in the time of ignorance with some men of Quraysh on trade to Syria. He said: I was in one of its markets when a Byzantine officer seized my neck. I tried to wrestle with him, but I was told: "Do not do so, for you have no share of him." He brought me into a church where there was a great heap of dust. He came to me with a basket and a shovel and said: "Move what is here." I began looking at how to do it. When it was midday he came to me wearing a garment through which I could see his whole body, and he said: "You have not moved anything, as I see." Then he clasped his hands and struck my skull with them. I said: "May your mother be bereaved, O 'Umar! Have you reached what I see?" Then I leapt to the shovel and struck his head with it, so that his brain spattered; I buried him in the dust and went out on my face, not knowing where I was going. I travelled the rest of that day and the following night until midday, and arrived at a monastery and sheltered in its courtyard. A man came out of it and said to me: "O servant of God, what keeps you sitting here?" I said: "I have lost my companions." He said: "You are not on the road, and you look at me with the eye of one afraid. Enter, eat some food and rest." I entered, and he brought me food and drink and fed me. Then he gazed at me steadily, and said: "By God, the People of the Book know that on earth there is none more knowledgeable of the Scripture than I. I see your description, the description that will drive us out of this monastery and overcome us." I said: "Sir, you have taken me in a direction other than I intended." He said: "What is your name?" I said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab." He said: "By God, you are our companion. Write for me a document concerning this monastery and what is in it." I said: "Sir, you have done me a kindness, so do not repeat it." He said: "It is only a document on parchment. If you are our companion, then so be it; if not, nothing will harm you." So I wrote him a document concerning his monastery and what is in it. He brought me clothes and dirhams and gave them to me, then he saddled a she-ass for me and said: "Do you see it?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Ride it, for you will not pass by any people without their giving it water and fodder and hosting you. When you reach your safe place, strike its face while it is turning away, for they will do that to it until it returns to me." I rode it, and it was as he said, until I caught up with my companions who were heading toward the Hijaz; I struck it while it turned away and went on with them.

When 'Umar came to Syria in his caliphate, that monk came to him with the document, and he was the abbot of the monastery of al-'Ars. When he saw him, he recognized him, and said: "There has come what 'Umar has no escape from." Then he turned to his companions and related to them his account. When he finished, he turned to the monk and said: "Do you have anything of benefit for the Muslims?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "If you host the Muslims, treat their sick and guide them, we will do so." He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful." 'Umar fulfilled his promise to him, may Allah be pleased with him and have mercy on him.

From Sayf, traced back to Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: When 'Umar entered Syria, a Jew of Damascus met him and said: "Peace be upon you, O Faruq, you are the master of Iliya'; by God, you will not return until God conquers Iliya'."

Among these: 'Amr ibn al-'As came to Madinah after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him to 'Uman as its governor. One day a Jew of the Jews of 'Uman came to him and said: "I adjure you by God, who sent you to us?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The Jew said: "By God, you know that he is the Messenger of Allah." 'Amr said: "Yes." The Jew said: "If what you say is true, he has died today." When 'Amr heard that, he gathered his companions and wrote down that very day which the Jew had said was the day the Prophet (ﷺ) died. Then he set out and was informed of the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) while on the road, and found that he had died on that very day (ﷺ), and blessed, honored and ennobled be he.

Among these: the delegation of Ghassan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq met them and said: "Who are you?" They said: "A group from Ghassan. We came to Muhammad to hear his speech." He said: "Lodge where delegations lodge, then go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and speak with him." They said: "Can we speak with him as we wish?" Abu Bakr smiled and said: "He walks in the markets, goes alone, has no guard with him, and whoever sees him is drawn to him." They said to Abu Bakr: "Who are you, sir?" He said: "I am Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah." They said: "Will you take charge of this affair after him?" Abu Bakr said: "The affair is in God's hands." He said to them: "How can you be deceived away from Islam when the People of the Book have informed you of his description, and that he is the last of the prophets?" Then they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and embraced Islam.

﴿He enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong﴾. It may be that this is part of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Torah, so the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun of the object in "they find him"; or it is an explanation of what was written of the mention; or it is a new description from God, exalted is He, not mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿And he makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the wicked things﴾. The view of Malik is that "the good things" are the lawful, and "the wicked things" are the unlawful. The view of al-Shafi'i is that "the good things" are the pleasant, and "the wicked things" are the repugnant, such as beetles, scorpions and others. ﴿And he relieves them of their burden﴾, and this is an image for the hardships imposed on them in their law, such as the killing of oneself as repentance, and cutting off the place of impurity from a garment; likewise "the shackles" are an expression for what their law prohibited, such as the forbidding of fats, and the prohibition of work on Saturday, and the like. ﴿And they honour him﴾, that is, they defended him with support so that no enemy could prevail over him. ﴿And they follow the light which has been sent down with him﴾: it is the Qur'an, or the whole law, and "with him" means with his mission and his messengership.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 158:

﴿Say, O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾. Its explanation is his (ﷺ) saying: "Every prophet was sent specifically to his own people, but I was sent to all of mankind." So the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of jamee'an (all) is that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring back to the pronoun in ilaykum (to you). ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: this is an adjective (na't) describing Allah, or it is in the accusative of praise by an implied verb, or in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject. ﴿There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet, who believes in Allah and His words﴾: "His words" are those which Allah revealed to him and to the other prophets. ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community﴾: they are those who remained steadfast when others wavered in the time of Musa, or those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) during his lifetime.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 160:

﴿And We divided them﴾ i.e., We separated them ﴿into twelve tribes﴾. Al-sibt (tribe) among the Children of Israel is like the qabilah (tribe) among the Arabs. Its placement (as an accusative) is as a substitute (badal) for "twelve," not as a specification (tamyiz), since the specification of "twelve" can only be singular. Al-Zamakhshari said it is a specification, because each tribe is asbat, not sibt. ﴿So there gushed forth﴾ i.e., burst forth. However, al-inbijas (a welling forth) is lighter than al-infijar (a bursting forth). Al-Qazwini said: al-inbijas is the beginning of al-infijar. ﴿And We shaded them with the clouds﴾, and what follows up to His words "for they used to wrong" is mentioned in al-Baqarah [2:57].

Note: There is a difference in wording between this passage in this surah and the passage in Surat al-Baqarah: in His words "infajarat" and "inbajasat," in His words "And when We said: Enter," and "And when it was said to them: Dwell," and in His words "wa-kulu" with the conjunction waw and "fa-kulu" with the conjunction fa. Al-Zamakhshari said: there is no harm in the difference of expression when there is no contradiction. Our shaykh, al-Ustadh Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr, explained them in his book Mulak al-Ta'wil, and the author of al-Durra gave explanations, some strong and some weak, and the discussion is lengthy, so we have left them because of their length.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 163:

﴿وَسْئَلْهُمْ﴾ That is: ask the Jews, by way of reproach and confrontation (taqrir wa-tawbikh). ﴿عَنِ ٱلْقَرْيَةِ﴾ [about the town]. It has been said: it is Iliya (Jerusalem). It has been said: it is Tiberias. It has been said: it is Madyan. ﴿حَاضِرَةَ ٱلْبَحْرِ﴾ [which was by the sea], near it or on its shore. ﴿إِذْ يَعْدُونَ فِي ٱلسَّبْتِ﴾ [when they transgressed in the Sabbath], that is, they exceeded the limit God set for it, which was their fishing on the Sabbath day, although they had been forbidden from it. The position of "idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "al-qaryah" (the town), and what is meant is its people. It is either a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), or it is in the accusative governed by "kanat" (was) or by "hadirah" (present/nearby). ﴿إِذْ تَأْتِيهِمْ حِيتَانُهُمْ يَوْمَ سَبْتِهِمْ شُرَّعاً﴾ [when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, openly visible]. The fish used to come out of the sea on the Sabbath day until they reached their houses, as a trial for them; since catching them was forbidden to them on the Sabbath day, and they would be absent from them on the other days. "Sabtahum" (their Sabbath) is a verbal noun (masdar) from your saying: "sabata al-Yahudi yasbutu" (the Jew observed the Sabbath), when he honored the Sabbath day. The meaning of "shurra'an" (openly visible): apparent, close to them; it is said: "shara'a minna fulan" (so-and-so drew near to us) when he approached. And "idh" in His words "idh ta'tihim" (when there came to them) is in the accusative governed by "ya'dun" (they transgress), or it is a substitute for "idh ya'dun" (when they transgressed).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 164–165:

﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?"﴾ (The verse): The Children of Israel split into three groups. One group disobeyed on the Sabbath by hunting. Another group forbade that and withdrew from the people. A third group remained silent and withdrew, neither forbidding nor disobeying. When this third group saw the defiance of the forbidding group's targets and the transgression of the disobedient ones, they said to the forbidding group, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish?" The forbidding group replied, "We admonish them as an excuse before our Lord, and so that perhaps they will fear Allah." The disobedient group was destroyed, and the forbidding group was saved. It is disputed whether the third group was destroyed for its silence or saved for its withdrawal and its abstention from disobedience. ﴿with a severe punishment﴾: that is, harsh. It is read with the hamza (بَئِيس, ba'is) and without it, and it is also read on the pattern fa'il (بَئِيس) and fay'al (بَيْئِس), and all of these derive from the meaning of bu's (بؤس), misery or hardship.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 166–167:

﴿فَلَماَّ عَتَوْاْ عَن مَّا نُهُواْ عَنْهُ﴾ That is, when they became arrogant toward what they had been forbidden. ﴿قُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُواْ قِرَدَةً خَٰسِئِينَ﴾ ("Then when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them: Be apes, despised and driven away.") This was mentioned in al-Baqarah [65]. The meaning is that they were first punished with a severe punishment, and when they persisted in defiance because of it, they were transformed into apes. It is also said: "when they persisted" repeats His saying "when they forgot," and the severe punishment (al-'adhab al-ba'is) is the transformation. ﴿تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكَ﴾ ("Your Lord declared") means He resolved, and it derives from ta'adhdhun (ئذان), in the sense of informing. ﴿لَيَبْعَثَنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("He will surely send against them") the verse onward, meaning He will empower over them; from this is the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax), and their humiliation throughout all lands.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 166–167:

﴿فَلَماَّ عَتَوْاْ عَن مَّا نُهُواْ عَنْهُ﴾ That is, when they became arrogant toward what they had been forbidden. ﴿قُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُواْ قِرَدَةً خَٰسِئِينَ﴾ ("Then when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them: Be apes, despised and driven away.") ﴿And We divided them up in the land﴾, meaning We scattered them through the towns, so that in every town there is a group of them, and they have no territory they can rule. ﴿Among them are the righteous﴾: they are those who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, or those among their earlier generations who were righteous. ﴿with good things and bad things﴾, meaning with blessings and afflictions.

**Qur'an 7:169:** ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession (khalf) who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower world and saying, "It will be forgiven us."﴾ Their meaning: a bad people came after them. Khalf with a sukun on the lam (khalf) is used in dispraise, and with a fatha on it (khalaf) in praise. The intended people are those from among the Jews who came after those already mentioned. It was also said that the intended people are the Christians.

﴿Taking the goods of this lower world﴾: that is, the goods (ʿaraḍ) of worldly life.

﴿And saying, "It will be forgiven us"﴾: this is their deception and their lying.

﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾: the waw here is for the circumstantial state (wa li-l-ḥāl), meaning they hope for forgiveness while they return to the likes of their deeds.

﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say about Allah except the truth?﴾: this is an indication of their lying in their saying "It will be forgiven us." As for the parsing (iʿrāb) of an-lā yaqūlū: it is either an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "the covenant of the Book," or an explanation (tafsīr) of it; or the an may be an explanatory particle (ḥarf ʿibāra wa tafsīr).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 170–171:

﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾. It has been read with the doubled (shaddah) and the single form, and both have the same meaning. As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab), "alladhina" is in apposition (ʿatf) to "alladhina yattaqun," or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿Indeed, We do not waste the reward of the righteous﴾. The mention of "the righteous" (al-muslihin) is placed in the position of a pronoun, because the righteous are those who hold fast to the Book. ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them﴾, meaning: We uprooted the mountain, lifted it above the Children of Israel, and said to them: "Take the Torah." This was when they refused to accept it. The explanation of "the canopy" (al-zullah) has already been given in al-Baqarah [93], and "Take what We have given you with strength."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 172:

﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying]: "Am I not your Lord?"﴾ The verse: regarding its meaning there are two opinions.

The first: that when Allah created Adam, He brought forth his descendants from his loins, like specks (dhurr), and took from them a covenant that He is their Lord, and they acknowledged this and bound themselves to it. This meaning has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) through many routes, and a group of the Companions and others held it.

The second: that this is a figure of speech (tamthil), and that "taking the descendants" is an expression for bringing them into existence in this world. As for "making them testify," its meaning is that Allah set up for the children of Adam proofs of His lordship, and their intellects bore witness to it; so it is as if He made them testify concerning themselves, and said to them: "Am I not your Lord?", and it is as if they said by the tongue of their state: "Yes, You are our Lord."

The first is the sound opinion because the reports about it are mutawatir (widely transmitted). However, the wording of the verse does not correspond to it on its apparent sense, which is why those who held the second opinion turned away from it. It corresponds to it only through interpretation (ta'wil). That is because the taking of the descendants occurred from the loins of Adam, whereas the wording of the verse implies that the taking of the descendants was from the children of Adam. The reconciliation between them is that the verse mentions "children of Adam" while meaning Adam himself, like His saying: "And We created you, then We fashioned you" (7:11), and the interpretation is: "We created your father Adam in his form."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the intended "children of Adam" are the forefathers of the Jews, and the intended "their descendants" are those who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). But in the well-known sound report, the intended meaning is the totality of the children of Adam, as we have mentioned.

﴿They said: "Yes, we testify"﴾: their saying "yes" is an acknowledgment from them that Allah is their Lord, for its estimated sense is: "You are our Lord." Since "bala" after a negative or affirmative confirmation (taqrir) implies affirmation, unlike "na'am" (yes), which when it follows a question implies affirmation, and when it follows a confirmation implies negation. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said regarding this verse: "Had they said 'na'am', they would have disbelieved." As for their saying "we testify," its meaning is: we testify to Your lordship; it is a confirmation of Allah's lordship and a discharge of their testimony thereof before Allah. It was also said: "we testify" is from the speech of Allah and the angels; i.e., we testify against the children of Adam through their acknowledgment. ﴿Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection﴾: it stands in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), i.e., "We did that lest you should say..." So it is from the speech of Allah, not from theirs. It was read with the ta' (you, addressing the children of Adam) and with the ya' (they, reporting about them).

He recited to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them. ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our verses, but he drew away from them﴾

Ibn Mas'ud said: He was a man from the Children of Israel, whom Musa (peace be upon him) sent to the king of Madyan, calling him to God. The king bribed him and gave him gifts on condition that he abandon the religion of Musa and follow the king in his religion, and he did so, and led people astray by that.

Ibn 'Abbas said: He was a man from the Canaanites named Bal'am ibn Ba'ura. He possessed the Greatest Name of God (ism Allah al-a'zam). When Musa intended to fight the Canaanites, who were the tyrants, they asked Bal'am to invoke the Greatest Name of God against Musa and his army. He refused, but they persisted with him until he invoked against them that they not enter the city, and Musa invoked against him.

According to this view, the signs that he was given are the Greatest Name of God. According to Ibn Mas'ud's view, they are what Musa taught him of the Sharia.

It was also said: He had with him some of the scrolls of Ibrahim.

Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: He was Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. He had been given knowledge and wisdom, and he wished to embrace Islam before the Battle of Badr, but then he turned back from that and died as a disbeliever. Concerning him the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt almost embraced Islam." According to this view, the sign is the knowledge that he had.

Infislakh (dissociation, detachment) is an expression for distancing and separation from them, like the stripping off of clothes or of skin.

﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾, that is, We would have raised his station by the signs that were with him. ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾ is an expression for his action, by which his station fell in the sight of God.

﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of the dog﴾, that is, his description is like the description of the dog, and this is extreme in baseness and vileness.

﴿If you drive him away, he pants, or if you leave him, he pants﴾. Luhath (panting) is rapid breathing, with movement of the mouth's organs and the tongue hanging out. It most often affects animals in heat and fatigue, and it is a constant state for the dog. The meaning of "if you drive him away" is if you do with him what burdens him, such as chasing him away or otherwise, or if you leave him without driving him away, he pants in every case. The point of comparing that man to it is that if you admonish him he is astray, and if you do not admonish him he is astray; his straying is in every case, just as the dog pants in every case.

It was also said: that man's tongue hung out upon his chest, so he became like the dog in his form and in his actual panting.

﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs﴾, that is, the description of those who deny is like the description of the dog in its panting, and like the description of the man who is compared to it, because if they are warned they are not guided, and if they are left they are not guided. He is compared to the man in that they saw the signs and miracles but they did not benefit them, just as the man was not benefited by the signs that he had.

﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs and their own selves﴾. The verse: this object was placed first for specification and restriction.

He recited to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them. ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our verses, but he drew away from them﴾

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 179:

﴿Many of the jinn and humankind﴾ are those whom God knew would enter the Fire because of their disbelief. So He informed that He created them for that, as in His saying: "These are for Paradise and I do not mind, and these are for the Fire and I do not mind." ﴿They have eyes with which they do not see﴾. The meaning is not the negation of hearing and sight altogether; rather, the meaning is the negation of them with respect to what benefits in religion.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 180:

﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise." The occasion of revelation of the verse: Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, heard some of the Companions reciting and mentioning Allah once as "Allah" and another time as "al-Rahman," so he said: "Muhammad claims that the God is one, and yet here he is worshipping many gods." So the verse was revealed clarifying that these many names all refer to one named Being. "Al-husna" is a feminine form (of the elative, "the most beautiful") or a verbal noun described by the adjective; the beauty of Allah's names is that they are attributes of praise, glorification and commendation. ﴿So call upon Him by them﴾, i.e., name Him by His names. Here is a permission to apply names to Allah the Exalted. As for those names that occur in the Qur'an or the Hadith, it is permissible to apply them to Allah by consensus (ijma' – scholarly agreement). As for those that have not been reported but which contain praise free of any suspicion of deficiency, Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib permitted applying them to Allah, while Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and others forbade that, holding that the names of Allah are restricted to what has been reported in the Qur'an and the Hadith. The book of al-Tirmidhi does mention their count, I mean the specification of the ninety-nine, and the scholars of hadith disagreed over whether those enumerated names in it are traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ) or are only the words of Abu Hurayrah. What is authentically reported in the Sahih is only that they are ninety-nine, without specification.

﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾ It was said: the meaning of "leave" (dharu) is: abandon them, do not argue with them and do not confront them; on this view the verse is abrogated by the command to fight. It was also said: the meaning of "leave" is warning and threat, like His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]; and this is the more apparent view given what follows it. Their deviation concerning Allah's names is what Abu Jahl said, for which the verse was revealed. It was also said: it is naming Him by what is not fitting. And it was said: it is naming idols by His name, like their deriving "al-Lat" from "Allah" and "al-Uzza" from "al-'Aziz."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 181–184:

﴿And among those We have created are a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ The verse: It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This verse is for you, and a similar one has already been mentioned concerning the people of Musa." ﴿We will gradually lead them [to destruction]﴾. Istidraj (gradual enticement) is a form of istif'al derived from daraja (degree), meaning: We drive them toward destruction little by little while they do not perceive it. Imla' (respite) is granting a delay while intending punishment. ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ He called His action toward them kayd (plan) because it resembles kayd in that its outward appearance is kindness while its inward reality is abandonment. ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion.﴾ "Their companion" means the Prophet (ﷺ), so He negated from him what the polytheists attributed to him of madness. It is possible that His saying "there is no madness in their companion" is the object of His saying "Have they not reflected," so that it is connected to it, and the meaning is: "Have they not reflected, so that they would know that there is no madness in your companion?" It is also possible that the speech is complete at His saying "Have they not reflected," and then He begins a new statement: "There is no madness in your companion." The first is better.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 185:

﴿Have they not considered﴾: meaning, consideration of inference (nazar istidlal). ﴿and what Allah has created﴾: this is conjoined to "the dominion" (al-malakut). By "thing" (shay') in His words "from any thing" he means all created beings, since all of them are evidence of the oneness of their Creator. ﴿and that it may be that their term has drawn near﴾: the first "an" (that) is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (muthaqqalah), and it is conjoined to "the dominion." The second "an" is the verbal (masdariyyah) particle in a position of nominative case after "asa" (it may be). "Ajaluhum" (their term) means their death. The meaning is: perhaps they will die soon, so it behoves them to hasten to consider that which will save them with Allah before the appointed term arrives. ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾: the pronoun ("this") refers to the Qur'an.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it come to pass?﴾ The askers were either the Jews or the Quraysh. The Resurrection is called "the Hour" because of the swiftness of its reckoning, as in His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer﴾. ﴿Ayyan mursaha﴾: *ayyan* means "when," and *mursaha* means its occurrence and coming into being. It derives from *irsa'*, meaning firmness and settling.

﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with God﴾: God has reserved the knowledge of its occurrence and has not disclosed it to anyone. ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾: *yujalliha* means to manifest it. It derives from *jalaa'*, the opposite of concealment. The *lam* in *liwaqtiha* is temporal (*zarfiyya*), meaning "at its time." The meaning is that none will manifest the Hour when its time comes except God.

﴿It has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾: there are three opinions regarding its meaning. First, it is heavy upon the people of the heavens and the earth because of its awesomeness for them and their fear of it. Second, it is heavy upon the heavens and the earth themselves, because the sky will be split open by it and the earth will be changed. Third, the meaning of "it has become heavy" is that its knowledge is heavy, i.e., hidden.

﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾: *al-hafiyy* with regard to a thing is one who is concerned with it and attentive to it. The meaning is: they ask you about it as though you were deeply concerned with knowing it. It has also been said that the meaning is: they ask you about it as though you were close to them because of your kinship with them, so that *'anha* ("about it") on these two views is connected to *yas'alunaka* ("they ask you"). It has also been said that the meaning is: they ask you as though you were eager to ask about it.

﴿Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much of good﴾: this is a disavowal of knowledge of the unseen and an argument for his not having such knowledge. ﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾: this is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with "I would have acquired much of good," meaning: had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good and guarded myself against harm. But I do not know it, so there befalls me what has been decreed for me of good and evil. It has also been said that his saying "and harm would not have touched me" is a resumptive statement (*istiʾnaf ikhbar*), and that "harm" here means madness; on this view, its connection to what precedes it is better.

﴿A people who believe﴾: this may be connected to both "a bringer of good tidings and a warner" together, meaning: give good tidings to the believers and warn them. Good tidings and warning are specified for them because they are the ones who benefit from them. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "good tidings" alone, with the object of "warner" omitted, meaning: a warner to the disbelievers. The first is better.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 189–191:**

﴿From a single soul﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿and created its mate﴾, meaning Hawwa' (Eve), ﴿so that he might find rest in her﴾, meaning that he might incline to her and find companionship with her. ﴿When he covered her﴾, a metaphor for intercourse. ﴿She bore a light burden﴾, meaning that it was light upon her and she did not suffer from it the harm and distress that some pregnant women suffer from their pregnancies. It was also said: the "light burden" is the semen in her womb. ﴿Then she went about with it﴾. It was said: this means she continued carrying it until its birth; it was also said: it means she stood and sat. ﴿Then when she became heavy﴾, meaning her burden grew heavy and she became heavy with it. ﴿If You give us a righteous one﴾, meaning a righteous child, sound in body. ﴿But when He gave them a righteous one﴾, meaning when He gave them a righteous child as they had asked: they made others as partners to Him concerning their children. The speech is therefore elliptical, with the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi, "the thing referred to") placed in the position of the thing it qualifies (al-mudaf). Likewise, in ﴿what He gave them﴾, meaning what He gave their children and descendants. It was also said: when Hawwa' became pregnant, Iblis came to her and said: "If you obey me and name what is in your womb ʿAbd al-Harith, I will save it for you, for Iblis's name was al-Harith. If you disobey me in this, I will kill it." She informed Adam of this, and he said to her: "He is our enemy who expelled us from the Garden." When she gave birth, the child died. Then she became pregnant a second time, and Iblis said to her the same thing, and she disobeyed him, and the child died. Then she became pregnant a third time, and they named him ʿAbd al-Harith, in hope of his survival. So His saying "they made others as partners to Him in what He gave them" means: in the naming only, not in worshipping other than God.

The first opinion is more sound for three reasons. First, it implies the innocence of Adam and his wife from even a small amount of shirk and from much of it, and this is the state of the prophets, peace be upon them. Second, it indicates that those who associated partners were the children of Adam and his descendants, based on the Most High's saying ﴿So exalted is God above what they associate with Him﴾, with the plural pronoun. Third, what they mention of the story of Adam and the naming of the child ʿAbd al-Harith requires transmission with a sound chain of narration, and this is not found in that story.

It was also said: ﴿From a single soul﴾ refers to Qusayy ibn Kilab and his wife, and ﴿they made others as partners to Him﴾ means they named their children ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, ʿAbd al-Dar and ʿAbd Manaf. This opinion is weak for two reasons. First, the address in this case would be specific to the descendants of Qusayy from Quraysh, whereas the apparent meaning is that the address is general to the children of Adam. Second, His saying "and from it He created its mate" applies to Hawwa', since she was created from Adam's rib, but does not apply to the wife of Qusayy.

﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ This verse is a refutation of the polytheists among the children of Adam. By His saying "what creates nothing" is meant the idols and whatever else is worshipped besides God. The meaning is that they are created and do not create, whereas God, the Most High, is the Creator who is not created; so He alone is the God.

Qur'an 7:192: "And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves."

This means that the idols cannot help those who worship them, nor can they help themselves. They are in utmost weakness and abasement, so how could they be gods?

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 193–196:

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you.﴾ Meaning: the idols do not respond when called, whether to be guided or to guide, because they are inanimate objects. ﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent.﴾ This is an emphasis and clarification of what precedes it. If it is asked: why did He say "am antum samitun" (or are you silent), placing a nominal sentence in the place of a verbal one, and why did He not say "aw samatum" (or you remained silent)? The answer is that your silence concerning calling upon the idols is a continuous state, so He expressed it with a nominal sentence, which requires continuity in that state. ﴿Indeed, those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you.﴾ This is a refutation of the polytheists, since their gods are servants; how then can a servant be worshipped alongside his Lord? ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾ This is a command in the mode of challenge (ta'jiz). ﴿Do they have feet by which they walk? Do they have hands by which they strike? Do they have eyes by which they see? Do they have ears by which they hear?﴾ [al-Shura: 21] (The text as given in the source reads: "Or do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?" [al-Shura: 21], and what follows it.) Its meaning is that the idols are inanimate objects lacking sense, limbs, life and power, and whoever is like this cannot be a god, for the attributes of a god include perception, life and power. This proof came in the form of a question because the polytheists themselves acknowledged that their idols do not walk, do not strike, do not see, and do not hear, so the proof was binding upon them. The hamza in His saying "a-lahum" is interrogative with reproach, and "am" in the three places has the sense of the hamza, with the meaning of "bal" (rather), and it is not conjunctive. ﴿Say: Call upon your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾ The meaning: seek help from your idols to harm me and to plot against me, and do not delay me, for you and your idols are unable to harm me. The purpose of the verse is to refute them by demonstrating the helplessness of their idols and their inability to cause harm, and it contains an indication of reliance upon Allah, seeking refuge in Him alone, and that other than Him has power over nothing. Then He made this explicit in His saying: ﴿Indeed my guardian is Allah﴾ and the verse that follows: that is, He is my protector and my helper against you, so you cannot harm me, even if you and your gods were to strive to harm me. Then He described Allah as the One who sent down the Book, and as the One who takes charge of the righteous. In these two attributes there is an argument for the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, by the sending down of the Book upon him, and that Allah has undertaken his protection; and whoever Allah undertakes to protect is among the righteous, and the righteous must be truthful in his speech, especially in what he says about Allah.

The answer is that your silence concerning calling upon the idols is a continuous state, so He expressed it with a nominal sentence, which requires continuity in that state. ﴿Indeed, those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you.﴾ This is a refutation of the polytheists, since their gods are servants; how then can a servant be worshipped alongside his Lord? ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾ This is a command in the mode of challenge (ta'jiz). ﴿Do they have feet by which they walk? Do they have hands by which they strike? Do they have eyes by which they see? Do they have ears by which they hear?﴾ [al-Shura: 21] (The text as given in the source reads: "Or do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?" [al-Shura: 21], and what follows it.) Its meaning is that the idols are inanimate objects lacking sense, limbs, life and power, and whoever is like this cannot be a god, for the attributes of a god include perception, life and power. This proof came in the form of a question because the polytheists themselves acknowledged that their idols do not walk, do not strike, do not see, and do not hear, so the proof was binding upon them. The hamza in His saying "a-lahum" is interrogative with reproach, and "am" in the three places has the sense of the hamza, with the meaning of "bal" (rather), and it is not conjunctive. ﴿Say: Call upon your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾ The meaning: seek help from your idols to harm me and to plot against me, and do not delay me, for you and your idols are unable to harm me. The purpose of the verse is to refute them by demonstrating the helplessness of their idols and their inability to cause harm, and it contains an indication of reliance upon Allah, seeking refuge in Him alone, and that other than Him has power over nothing. Then He made this explicit in His saying: ﴿Indeed my guardian is Allah﴾ and the verse that follows: that is, He is my protector and my helper against you, so you cannot harm me, even if you and your gods were to strive to harm me. Then He described Allah as the One who sent down the Book, and as the One who takes charge of the righteous. In these two attributes there is an argument for the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, by the sending down of the Book upon him, and that Allah has undertaken his protection; and whoever Allah undertakes to protect is among the righteous, and the righteous must be truthful in his speech, especially in what he says about Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 197–198:

﴿And those whom you invoke besides Him cannot help you﴾ [etc.]: This is a refutation of the polytheists, and its meaning has already been explained. ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear﴾. It may be that He means the idols, in which case this is a belittling of them and a refutation of those who worship them, for they are inanimate objects that hear nothing, so the meaning is like that which has already been mentioned. Or He means the disbelievers, and describing them as not hearing means not hearing in a way that benefits them, due to their extreme aversion, or because Allah has sealed their hearts. ﴿And you see them looking at you, yet they do not see﴾. If this is a description of the idols, then His saying "looking" (yanzuruna) is metaphorical, and His saying "they do not see" (la yubsiruna) is literal, because they have the form of eyes but see nothing with them. If it is a description of the disbelievers, then "looking" is literal and "they do not see" is metaphorical, in the manner of emphasis, just as He described them as not hearing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 199:

﴿Take to forgiveness﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: the meaning is, take from people in their character, their speech and their dealings whatever is easy, not what is burdensome for them, lest they become repelled. So "al-'afw" (forgiveness/ease) on this view means ease, and overlooking their faults. It is the opposite of ignorance and burdening, as in the saying of the poet:

"Take forgiveness from me, and your affection will endure."

The second: the meaning is, from charities, take what is easy for people in their wealth, or what is surplus to them. This was before the obligation of zakat was imposed. So "al-'afw" on this view means what is easy, or means abundance. ﴿And enjoin what is customary﴾, i.e., al-ma'ruf, which is doing good. It was said that al-'afw here means the customary practice prevailing among people. The Malikis used this verse to argue for ruling according to custom (al-'awa'id). ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, i.e., do not repay the foolish with the like of their words or deeds, and bear patiently with them. When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked Jibril about it. He said: "I do not know until I ask." Then he returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join ties with those who cut you off, to give to those who withhold from you, and to pardon those who wrong you." It is also related from Ja'far al-Sadiq: God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) in it with noble character. On this view its ruling remains established, and this is the sound opinion. It was also said that it was a means of conciliating the disbelievers, and then it was abrogated by fighting.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 200–201:

﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should provoke you, then seek refuge in Allah.﴾ The "nazgh" of Satan is his whispering, by casting doubt upon the truth and commanding acts of disobedience, or by stirring up anger. So Allah commanded seeking refuge from him at that time, as is related in the hadith that a man's anger intensified, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I know a word which, if he said it, what he feels would leave him: 'We seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed.'"

﴿A visitation from Satan﴾ means a passing thought (lamma) from him, as in what has come: "Indeed Satan has a passing thought and the angel has a passing thought." As for one who reads "ṭāʾif" with an alif, it is an active participle (ism fāʿil); and one who reads "ṭayf" with a silent yāʾ, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) or a lightened form of the intensified "ṭayyif," like "mayyit" and "mayt." ﴿Remember﴾: its object is omitted so that it covers everything that is remembered of the fear of Allah's punishment, or the hope of His reward, or His watchfulness and shame before Him, or the enmity of Satan and seeking refuge from him, and reflection and contemplation, and other things. ﴿Then behold, they see clearly﴾: this is from the insight of the heart.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verses 202–203:

﴿Their brothers (in error) keep extending them in deviation﴾. The pronoun in "their brothers" refers to the devils (shayatin). By his words "a visitation from Satan" he means the category (jins), which is why the plural pronoun is returned to it. "Their brothers" are the disbelievers. The meaning of "yumidduna-hum" (they supply them) is that they become a supply for them, that they strengthen them. The object pronoun in "yumiddunahum" refers to the disbelievers, and the subject pronoun refers to the devil. It is also possible that by "the brothers" he means the devils, and that the pronoun in "their brothers" refers to the disbelievers. The meaning in both cases is that the devil supplies the disbelievers. It is recited as "yumiddunahum" with a dammah and with a fathah on the ya', and the meaning is the same. "Fi al-ghayy" (in deviation) is connected to "yumiddunahum". It has also been said that it is connected to "ikhwanuhum", as when you say "ikhwah fi Allah" (brothers in God) or "fi al-shaytan" (in Satan).

﴿Then they do not hold back﴾, that is, the devils do not hold back from supplying their disbelieving brothers, or the disbelievers do not hold back from their deviation. In this verse there is, from the perception of eloquence (idrak al-bayan), the figure known as luzum ma la yalzam (the obligation of what is not obligatory), through the obligation of the sad before the ra' in "mubsirun" and "la yaqsirun".

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not devised it?"﴾. The pronoun in "lam ta'tihim" refers to the disbelievers. "Lawla" here is a substitute (iwad), and regarding the meaning of "ijtabaytaha" (devised it) there are two views. The first: you invented it from yourself, so the sign in this case is from the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ would sometimes be delayed in receiving revelation, and the disbelievers would say: "Why did you not bring a Qur'an from your own speech?" The second: its meaning is that you requested it from God and chose it over Him, so the sign in this case is a miracle, that is, they say: "Ask God for a miracle."

﴿Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord"﴾ (al-Jinn: 20). Its meaning: I do not invent the Qur'an according to the first view, and I do not request a sign from God according to the second view.

﴿This is insights﴾, that is, signs of guidance. The reference is to the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 7, verse 204–206:

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: the silence commanded is for the recitation of the imam in the prayer. The second: it is silence for the khutbah (sermon). The third: it is silence for the recitation of the Qur'an in general, and this is the preferred view, for two reasons. The first: the wording is general and there is no evidence restricting it. The second: the verse is Meccan, whereas the khutbah was only instituted in Medina.

﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾. Some of them said: mercy is closest to the listener of the Qur'an by this verse.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. It may mean remembrance by the heart rather than the tongue, or remembrance by the tongue quietly. According to the first, his words "and without loudness in speech" are a conjunction of different state, meaning another condition; according to the second, they are an explanation and clarification of the first.

﴿In the mornings and the evenings﴾. That is, in the morning and the afternoon and evening. Al-Aṣāl is the plural of uṣul, and al-uṣul is the plural of aṣīl. It is said: what is meant is the Subh (dawn) and 'Asr prayers. It is said: the obligatory five prayers. The more apparent view is the general sense.

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾: they are the angels, peace be upon them. Mentioning them is an encouragement to the believers and a rebuke to the disbelievers.

﴿And to Him they prostrate﴾. The prepositional phrase is placed first for the sake of the meaning of restriction, i.e., they prostrate only to Allah. And Allah knows best.
